title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

reading.body:
This is an access-control failure rather than a model failure. A person with legitimate credentials to law enforcement systems is alleged to have used them for a purpose the systems were not deployed for: personal tracking of a woman. The tools named, a Flock camera system, a tag reader system and the Georgia Crime Information Center database, are built to serve police work, and the alleged misuse happened inside that authorised access, not through any break in the technology.

The failure sits at the point where a query is made and a result is returned. Nothing in the reporting describes a technical safeguard that flagged the queries as personal rather than professional, and the conduct is alleged to have continued across two months. Catching this kind of misuse requires auditing who searched for whom and why, and treating a pattern of queries about one person as a signal, not as routine traffic.

What is not established is guilt. The eight counts are indictments returned by a grand jury, which is an accusation, not a finding, and the case had not reached trial at the time of the report.

reports.title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

summary:
A former Coffee County sheriff's deputy, Chris Ashley Rozar, 49, has been released on bond after a grand jury indicted him on eight counts, including four counts of violating his oath, two counts of computer invasion of privacy, one count of prohibited use of captured license plate data, and one count of stalking. Prosecutors allege that between April and May 2024, Rozar misused the sheriff's office Flock camera system, tag reader system, and the Georgia Crime Information Center database for personal reasons, including tracking and surveilling a woman without her consent. He was arrested on May 5 and released on bond the same day.

The woman at the center of the allegations spoke anonymously to WALB, saying she waited two years for the investigation and hopes her story encourages other women to report abuse. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation led the multi-year investigation after former Sheriff Doyle Wooten requested it in 2024, and Rozar was fired when it began. Rozar is scheduled for arraignment on May 27 in Coffee County Superior Court.
